tfn.s: The writer treats a tracker that supports a doctor's judgement differently from one that replaces it.
tfn.why: The text says: "The distinction lies in whether measurements inform judgement or replace it."

tfn.s: The writer suggests that a person whose sleep problems persist can safely rely on tracker data alone.
tfn.why: The text says such problems need assessment "not just a consumer algorithm."

tfn.s: Most sleep-tracker manufacturers fund their own research into accuracy.
tfn.why: The text does not say who pays for research.

tfn.s: A person who feels fine after a poor score may end up noticing tiredness they would otherwise ignore.

tfn.s: The writer sees measuring sleep as an isolated trend rather than part of a wider cultural pattern.
tfn.why: The text says: "The deeper issue is cultural. We increasingly quantify ordinary human experiences, from exercise to productivity and recovery."

speak.title: Role-play: should we try a sleep tracker?
speak.setup: Work in pairs. Read your card, then have the conversation. Swap roles and do it again.

a.text: You wear a smartwatch and check your sleep score every morning. You think the numbers help you. Explain why, and try to persuade your partner to wear one for a week.

b.text: You don't use a tracker. You think scores can make people worry. Ask questions, say what worries you, then decide: yes, no, or yes with a condition.

phrases: I check my score every morning.
It helps me see my habits.
Don't you think it can make you worry?
I'm not sure the numbers are always right.
I'd try it for a week if I didn't have to check it daily.
Could we agree on one week and then talk again?
speak.after: Afterwards, tell the class: will your partner try a tracker, and why?
